title: Improving the Welfare of Pangasius Catfish: Assessing the Effects of Transport Duration on Larval and Fingerling Survival Rates in the Mekong Delta, Vietnam
content: Live transport is a critical component of fish hatchery and nursery operations, particularly when larvae are transferred from hatcheries to nursery facilities. This study evaluated the effects of larval age at transport (24, 48, and 96 hours post-hatch), transport duration (3, 5, 7, and 10 hours), and oxygen management on the post-transport survival and subsequent nursery performance of Pangasius catfish. Three complementary experiments were conducted. In Experiment 1, larvae transported at earlier developmental stages (24–48 hours post-hatch) and for shorter durations (3–5 hours) exhibited significantly higher immediate post-transport survival. In Experiment 2, survival after 10 days of nursery rearing in hapa nets ranged from 12.4% to 23.9% among treatments. These values were 1.5–2.0 times higher than survival rates commonly reported by nursery farmers at 1–2 weeks after transport. Experiment 3 evaluated longer-term survival after 25 days of nursery rearing and confirmed the strong effects of both larval age and transport duration. The research also found that without oxygen replenishment, the highest survival rate (49.7 ± 4.7%) was achieved when larvae were transported within 24 hours post-hatch for no longer than 3 h, whilst oxygen replenishment at 3h intervals further increased survival to 55.3 ± 7.8%. Overall, transporting larvae at an early developmental stage, minimizing transport duration, and maintaining adequate oxygen levels substantially improved post-transport survival and subsequent nursery performance. These practices may therefore enhance production efficiency and fish welfare in Pangasius catfish aquaculture production.
